courses.title: Computing Foundations
courses.subtitle: From bits to programs, without the noise.
courses.description: A compact studio on how computers actually work. Watch a short lecture, sit with a reading, then prove the idea with a quiz. Drop in your own JSON later — this course is here so the room is already usable.

modules.title: The machine
modules.summary: What a computer is doing when it appears to think.

lessons.title: Early Computing
lessons.description: A brisk tour of how we got from mechanical calculators to stored programs.

lessons.title: Electronic Computing
lessons.description: Tubes, transistors, and why switching so fast changed everything.

lessons.title: Studio reading: a sample paper
lessons.description: Practice the PDF viewer with a public research PDF. Replace this URL with your own notes.

modules.title: Check the work
modules.summary: A short quiz with answers so you can see scoring and review.

lessons.title: Foundations check
lessons.description: Graded. Answers are included in the JSON so students get instant results.

questions.prompt: A stored-program computer keeps both data and instructions in memory. Why does that matter?

options.text: It lets the machine rewrite its own instructions and run different software without rewiring.
It means the computer can only run one program, burned into hardware.
It removes the need for memory entirely.
It is only useful for graphics cards.

questions.explanation: The stored-program idea is why software exists as a separate thing from the machine.

questions.prompt: Which pair best describes the leap from mechanical to electronic computing?

options.text: Bigger gears, slower clocks.
Switches that could flip millions of times a second.
Paper tape as the only storage.
Human computers remaining faster than machines.

questions.explanation: Electronics made switching cheap and fast. Speed is the whole plot.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that is true of a typical CPU.

options.text: It fetches instructions from memory.
It executes those instructions in a cycle.
It is mainly a display for the operating system.
It uses registers as tiny, fast scratch space.

questions.explanation: Fetch, decode, execute — with registers as the desk, not the warehouse.

courses.title: Generative AI Literacy
courses.subtitle: Watch the lecture. Read the paper. Then write what you know.
courses.description: A student path through large language models: what they are, how attention works, and how to think about them without the marketing fog. One quiz here has no answer key — the same shape your JSON can use until results are ready.

modules.title: The paper on the desk

modules.title: Prove it on paper

lessons.title: Practice — no answer key
lessons.description: Submitted locally. There are no correctOptionIds, so this is how your JSON can ship before results exist.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, what is an LLM predicting when it writes the next token?

options.text: The most likely next piece of text given the context so far.
A guaranteed true fact from a database.
The user’s private files.
A compiled computer program.

questions.prompt: Which habit is safest when you use a model for coursework?

options.text: Paste the output as-is; models do not err.
Treat it as a draft partner, then verify against sources you trust.
Ask it to invent citations if you are short on time.
Disable your own judgment because the model is larger than you.

lessons.title: Literacy check
lessons.description: Graded. Instant review when the JSON includes results.

options.text: Look only at the previous token, like a Markov chain.
Weight other tokens in the context when building its representation.
Skip memory and jump straight to the file system.
Guarantee factual accuracy.

questions.explanation: Attention is a weighted look at the context, not a truth oracle.

questions.prompt: Pretraining a language model is closest to:

options.text: Teaching it one company handbook.
Next-token prediction on a very large text corpus.
Labeling every sentence as true or false.
Compressing images with JPEG.

questions.explanation: Scale plus next-token prediction is the pretraining recipe.

options.text: A fluent answer can still be wrong.
Temperature changes how sharply the model samples.
Models always cite real papers.
Context windows limit how much you can stuff into one prompt.

questions.explanation: Fluency ≠ truth. Sampling is tunable. Context is finite. Citations are often invented.
